etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ministre, from Old French ministre, from Latin minister (“an attendant, servant, assistant, a priest's assistant or other under official”), from minor (“less”) + -ter; see minor. Doublet of Minorite.

definitions.definition: (Protestantism) A person who is trained to preach, to perform religious ceremonies, and to afford pastoral care at a Protestant church.
(Roman Catholicism) A person (either a layperson or an ordained clergy member) who is commissioned to perform some act on behalf of the Catholic Church.
(government) A politician who heads a ministry

quote.citation: 1661 (first printed), Francis Bacon, A Letter of Advice to the Duke of Buckingham:
quote.text: Ministers to kings, whose eyes, ears, and hands they are, must be answerable to God and man.

Hypernym: provost (chief minister in areas of Central Europe and Scandinavia)

definitions.definition: In diplomacy, the rank of diplomat directly below ambassador.
A servant; a subordinate; an officer or assistant of inferior rank; hence, an agent, an instrument.

quote.citation: c. 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Winters Tale”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii], page 287, column 2:
quote.text: […], I choſe / Camillo for the miniſter, to poyſon / My friend Polixenes:  […]

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 24:13, column 1:
quote.text: And Moſes roſe vp, and his miniſter Ioſhua: and Moſes went vp into the mount of God.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English mynystren, from Middle French ministrer, from Old French menistrer, ministrer and Latin ministrō, from minister.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To attend to (the needs of); to tend; to take care (of); to give aid; to give service.
(intransitive) To function as a clergyman or as the officiant in church worship.
(transitive, archaic) To afford, to give, to supply.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i], page 7, column 2:
quote.text: I do vvell beleeue your Highneſſe, and did it to miniſter occaſion to theſe Gentlemen,  […](to give opportunity to these gentlemen)

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Corinthians 9:10, column 2:
quote.text: ( […]  Now he that miniſtreth ſeede to the ſower, both miniſter bread for your foode, and multiply your ſeede ſowen, and encreaſe the fruites of your righteouſneſſe)

quote.citation: 1651–1653, Jer[emy] Taylor, ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΣ [Eniautos]. A Course of Sermons for All the Sundays of the Year. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Richard Royston […], published 1655, →OCLC:
quote.text: We minister to God reason to suspect us.
